summary: We developed an illustrated educational comic titled "Silent Sentinels: NASA’s Legacy Hardware — Ghost Fleet of the Moon," which chronicles the historic missions of NASA’s Surveyor 3 lander and the Apollo 12 astronauts who visited it. This project addresses the challenge of transforming technical spaceflight history and materials-science findings into an engaging, accessible visual narrative for students and the general public. By illustrating how engineers recovered and analyzed spacecraft components after 31 months of exposure on the lunar surface, the project highlights why studying legacy hardware is critical for designing durable, radiation-resistant spacecraft for modern lunar exploration initiatives like the Artemis program.
details:
Project Details

  • What it does / How it works:
    • The project uses a six-panel sequential comic format to tell a chronological story. It begins with Surveyor 3 landing in the Ocean of Storms in April 1967 to test lunar soil firmness and capture 6,300 photographs before losing power. It then depicts Apollo 12’s pinpoint landing in November 1969, where astronauts visited the dormant probe and cut off hardware pieces—such as the television camera—for Earth-based laboratory analysis.
    • Benefits: Makes complex aerospace engineering concepts—such as space radiation degradation, vacuum exposure, and micrometeorite pitting—easy to visualize and understand.
    • Intended Impact: To inspire public interest in space history and demonstrate how past lunar missions directly inform the engineering safety and durability of future Artemis missions.
    • Developed using historical mission records and laboratory photographs from NASA alongside digital illustration and graphic layout software to create the comic panels, typography, and magnified scientific inset.
    • The team creatively blended classic comic-book aesthetics (bold action captions, sound effects like "SNIP!", and dramatic framing) with real scientific data, including a magnified inset of micrometeorite pits on Surveyor 3's paint. Key considerations included historical accuracy, clear visual pacing, and connecting 1960s space exploration to modern Artemis goals.
